messages.subject: Phylogenetic PCA + use of data that is corrected for phylogenetic signal
parts:
Hi Geomorph community,

In my dataset on distal ulnar shape I want to check for a phylogenetic signal and, if present, I want to correct for a phylogenetic signal in the subsequent analyses. I have a few questions/remarks about this as I have no experience using phylogeny in data-analysis (and reading all the different approaches freaks me out a little bit ...).

1) To run a phylogenetic PCA, I have to use the mean shape of the different primate taxa in combination with a phylogenetic tree (which shows the same taxa). I did some research on how to perform this in R, and I came across this description (Almecija, 2015):

"To assess the phylogenetic patterning in the shape space, we mapped a phylogenetic tree onto the shape space defined by the two first axes of a PCA of the covariance
matrix of extant taxa means. Hypothetical ancestral states (internal nodes in the tree) were reconstructed using squared-change parsimony (Maddison, 1991) with a method developed for geometric data in which shape is treated as a single multidimensional
character and weighed by branch length (Klingenberg and Gidaszewski, 2010). Subsequently, the estimated ancestral node configurations were plotted on the original
shape space, and the branches of the tree were connected to obtain a phylomorphospace (Rohlf, 2002; Sidlauskas, 2008; Monteiro, 2013)."

I have to admit that, since I'm not familiar with using phylogeny in PCA analyses, this is hard for me to follow. According to this description, I cannot simply use a phylogenetic tree in combination with mean shapes, and additional parameters need to be added to get a proper phylogenetic PCA?

2) If there is a phylogenetic signal in the dataset, I want to correct for it because I have to use phylogenetic-corrected data in the subsequent analyses. Is it possible to do this without having to use mean shapes in the subsequent analyses? Because this means losing all the variance, which would then prevent from testing differences between the species themselves ... Most tools seem to assume that, when you want to control for phylogeny, you are testing according to a different grouping variable that is not the species itself (e.g. locomotor groups)?

In the paper mentioned above, this is what is said in the method section:

"The previous steps were necessary to subsequently test for the presence of a phylogenetic signal in hamate shape space by means of a permutation test approach (Laurin, 2004) extended for multivariate analysis of coordinate data (Klingenberg and Gidaszewski, 2010). This technique simulates the null hypothesis of complete absence of phylogenetic structure among hamate shapes in extant anthropoids. The species mean shape configurations were randomly distributed as the TIPS of the phylogeny in 10,000 permutations. For each permutation, tree length (i.e., the sum of the squared Procrustes distances between ancestral and descendant shapes for all branches) was computed. If more than 5% of the resulting tree lengths computed in the permutation test were greater than the one obtained with the original data, the null hypothesis of absence of phylogenetic structure in the data was rejected."

Again, as I'm not familiar with the different terms, I don't really understand. Is the function "phylosig" OK to use to test for a phylogenetic signal? And I also don't see HOW they corrected the data for the phylogenetic signal.

I'm very sorry for my extensive question. I'm quite new in the field, and people saying "It's not that difficult' do not help either ... In general, it would be nice if someone here would be happy to help me (e.g. during a skype call) with these analyses. I have a full R script for my PCA analyses, 2B-PLS analyses, ... but I can really use some guidance on how to properly implement phylogeny into this story. Of course, you can be co-author on the publication (will normally be published in a Mary Marzke special issue of the American Journal of Biological Anthropology).

Thank you very much.

Marie.

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Phylogenetic PCA + use of data that is corrected for phylogenetic signal
parts:
Marie,

 

The descriptions from the papers you cited are correct, but one does not need to do all of those steps by hand. For instance, the function ‘gm.prcomp’ in geomorph will provide ordinations of one’s data, and if you provide the function with a phylogeny, it will allow you to obtain one of 3 ordinations with phylogeny: 1 a phylomorphospace (a PCA with the phylogeny projected into that space), a phylogenetic-PCA (ala Revell 2009), or a PACA plot: phylogenetically aligned components analysis (ala Collyer and Adams 2021). Note that projecting the phylogeny into the PCA is NOT a phylogenetic-PCA (as you stated). It instead is a phylomorphospace. Phylogenetic PCA accounts for the phylogeny during the rotation step.  Give a careful read to Collyer and Adams 2021 who describe all 3 approaches.


For phylogenetic signal, one can evaluate this using the function physignal.  This using Kmult, the multivariate generalization of Blomberg’s kappa (Adams 2014). It is not the same procedure as described in Klingenberg’s paper, which is discussed in my paper.

 

For PLS, one can account for the phylogeny using phylo.integration; again in geomorph.


Note that one really should read the primary literature and understand what these methods and approaches are doing mathematically. We have several review papers on multivariate phylogenetic comparative methods (Adams and Collyer 2018, 2019) which are available on my web page. They survey many of these and other approaches.


Best,

 

Dean

parts:
Dear Dean,

Thank you for your reply. I indeed came across your 2021 paper on the different methods and if I understand correctly, what I basically need to do (for both phy-PCA or PACA) is:
- I use phylosignal to test for a phylogenetic signal in the dataset (which can run both the lambda and K on PC scores)
- as a complement to that, I can run a PGLS and test the effect of phylogeny in my sample
- if this is significant, I do a PCA with the residuals of that test and get phylogenetically corrected data to work with

BUT, what confuses me is that when I implement a phylogenetic tree into the function this would mean that I need to work with mean shapes, no? Otherwise the number of datapoints won't match with the number of tips of the tree. And using mean shapes implies losing all variance between the different specimens? Or maybe this does not matter because I can use the residuals in the subsequent PCA analyses and test for significant differences between the different specimens.

And what I understand from your paper is that, because PACA shows variations most associated with phylogenetic signal while in phy-PCA this is most independent of phylogenetic variation, it would be best to use both tests next to each other.

All the best,
Marie

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Phylogenetic PCA + use of data that is corrected for phylogenetic signal
parts:
Marie,

 

Yes, phylogenetic comparative methods all require that there is a ‘match’ between the data and the phylogeny. Thus, since there is one tip per species, one requires one data point. That is typically the mean of a sample of specimens for that species. Some other points of corection

 

PGLS tests for associations between dependent (Y) and independent (X) variables while accounting for phylogeny. It was unclear what you were testing (you need both X and Y variables)

 

One does not need to do a PCA with residuals of the PGLS, though many papers do this; thinking that they are working with phylogenetically ‘corrected’ data. I do not prefer that term, and prefer to work with pPCA and PACA which includes the data and the phylogeny directly in the ordination.

Dean

Marie.

Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Phylogenetic PCA + use of data that is corrected for phylogenetic signal

 

Hi Geomorph community,

 

In my dataset on distal ulnar shape I want to check for a phylogenetic signal and, if present, I want to correct for a phylogenetic signal in the subsequent analyses. I have a few questions/remarks about this as I have no experience using phylogeny in data-analysis (and reading all the different approaches freaks me out a little bit ...).

 

1) To run a phylogenetic PCA, I have to use the mean shape of the different primate taxa in combination with a phylogenetic tree (which shows the same taxa). I did some research on how to perform this in R, and I came across this description (Almecija, 2015):

 

"To assess the phylogenetic patterning in the shape space, we mapped a phylogenetic tree onto the shape space defined by the two first axes of a PCA of the covariance

matrix of extant taxa means. Hypothetical ancestral states (internal nodes in the tree) were reconstructed using squared-change parsimony (Maddison, 1991) with a method developed for geometric data in which shape is treated as a single multidimensional
character and weighed by branch length (Klingenberg and Gidaszewski, 2010). Subsequently, the estimated ancestral node configurations were plotted on the original
shape space, and the branches of the tree were connected to obtain a phylomorphospace (Rohlf, 2002; Sidlauskas, 2008; Monteiro, 2013)."

 

I have to admit that, since I'm not familiar with using phylogeny in PCA analyses, this is hard for me to follow. According to this description, I cannot simply use a phylogenetic tree in combination with mean shapes, and additional parameters need to be added to get a proper phylogenetic PCA?

 

2) If there is a phylogenetic signal in the dataset, I want to correct for it because I have to use phylogenetic-corrected data in the subsequent analyses. Is it possible to do this without having to use mean shapes in the subsequent analyses? Because this means losing all the variance, which would then prevent from testing differences between the species themselves ... Most tools seem to assume that, when you want to control for phylogeny, you are testing according to a different grouping variable that is not the species itself (e.g. locomotor groups)?

In the paper mentioned above, this is what is said in the method section:

"The previous steps were necessary to subsequently test for the presence of a phylogenetic signal in hamate shape space by means of a permutation test approach (Laurin, 2004) extended for multivariate analysis of coordinate data (Klingenberg and Gidaszewski, 2010). This technique simulates the null hypothesis of complete absence of phylogenetic structure among hamate shapes in extant anthropoids. The species mean shape configurations were randomly distributed as the TIPS of the phylogeny in 10,000 permutations. For each permutation, tree length (i.e., the sum of the squared Procrustes distances between ancestral and descendant shapes for all branches) was computed. If more than 5% of the resulting tree lengths computed in the permutation test were greater than the one obtained with the original data, the null hypothesis of absence of phylogenetic structure in the data was rejected."

Again, as I'm not familiar with the different terms, I don't really understand. Is the function "phylosig" OK to use to test for a phylogenetic signal? And I also don't see HOW they corrected the data for the phylogenetic signal.

 

I'm very sorry for my extensive question. I'm quite new in the field, and people saying "It's not that difficult' do not help either ... In general, it would be nice if someone here would be happy to help me (e.g. during a skype call) with these analyses. I have a full R script for my PCA analyses, 2B-PLS analyses, ... but I can really use some guidance on how to properly implement phylogeny into this story. Of course, you can be co-author on the publication (will normally be published in a Mary Marzke special issue of the American Journal of Biological Anthropology).

 

Thank you very much.

 

Marie.

parts: When using means, the only thing potentially ‘masked’ is within-species variation (not differences). However, understand that since your phylogeny is at the species level, it only contains information about the species, not individuals within the species. Thus, using the mean shape is the only way to match them up.

Dean

Dear Dean,

 

Ah yes I'm sorry, we used the different primate genera as independent categorical variable and size as a covariate. So we want to test for the effect of size on shape while accounting for phylogeny.

I indeed found a lot of papers using the residuals afterwards, which was also suggested by the reviewer of our paper for us to do in the subsequent analyses, so thank you for clearing that up!

However, the fact that we need to work with mean species shapes in the pPCA and PACA does not pose a problem when investigating significant differences between the different species themselves? Because in a regular PCA all datapoints are present separately and I always thought that creating a mean shape could imply 'masking' more subtle shape differences.

 

Marie.

 

Op vrijdag 16 december 2022 om 10:54:07 UTC+1 schreef dca...@iastate.edu:

Marie,

 

Yes, phylogenetic comparative methods all require that there is a ‘match’ between the data and the phylogeny. Thus, since there is one tip per species, one requires one data point. That is typically the mean of a sample of specimens for that species. Some other points of corection

 

PGLS tests for associations between dependent (Y) and independent (X) variables while accounting for phylogeny. It was unclear what you were testing (you need both X and Y variables)

 

One does not need to do a PCA with residuals of the PGLS, though many papers do this; thinking that they are working with phylogenetically ‘corrected’ data. I do not prefer that term, and prefer to work with pPCA and PACA which includes the data and the phylogeny directly in the ordination.

 

Dean

Dear Dean,

 

Thank you for your reply. I indeed came across your 2021 paper on the different methods and if I understand correctly, what I basically need to do (for both phy-PCA or PACA) is:

- I use phylosignal to test for a phylogenetic signal in the dataset (which can run both the lambda and K on PC scores)

- as a complement to that, I can run a PGLS and test the effect of phylogeny in my sample

- if this is significant, I do a PCA with the residuals of that test and get phylogenetically corrected data to work with

 

BUT, what confuses me is that when I implement a phylogenetic tree into the function this would mean that I need to work with mean shapes, no? Otherwise the number of datapoints won't match with the number of tips of the tree. And using mean shapes implies losing all variance between the different specimens? Or maybe this does not matter because I can use the residuals in the subsequent PCA analyses and test for significant differences between the different specimens.

 

And what I understand from your paper is that, because PACA shows variations most associated with phylogenetic signal while in phy-PCA this is most independent of phylogenetic variation, it would be best to use both tests next to each other.

 

All the best,

Marie

Op donderdag 15 december 2022 om 18:26:35 UTC+1 schreef dca...@iastate.edu:

Marie,

 

The descriptions from the papers you cited are correct, but one does not need to do all of those steps by hand. For instance, the function ‘gm.prcomp’ in geomorph will provide ordinations of one’s data, and if you provide the function with a phylogeny, it will allow you to obtain one of 3 ordinations with phylogeny: 1 a phylomorphospace (a PCA with the phylogeny projected into that space), a phylogenetic-PCA (ala Revell 2009), or a PACA plot: phylogenetically aligned components analysis (ala Collyer and Adams 2021). Note that projecting the phylogeny into the PCA is NOT a phylogenetic-PCA (as you stated). It instead is a phylomorphospace. Phylogenetic PCA accounts for the phylogeny during the rotation step.  Give a careful read to Collyer and Adams 2021 who describe all 3 approaches.


For phylogenetic signal, one can evaluate this using the function physignal.  This using Kmult, the multivariate generalization of Blomberg’s kappa (Adams 2014). It is not the same procedure as described in Klingenberg’s paper, which is discussed in my paper.

 

For PLS, one can account for the phylogeny using phylo.integration; again in geomorph.


Note that one really should read the primary literature and understand what these methods and approaches are doing mathematically. We have several review papers on multivariate phylogenetic comparative methods (Adams and Collyer 2018, 2019) which are available on my web page. They survey many of these and other approaches.


Best,

 

Dean
